title: A Comparative Study of Unmanned Surface Vessel and Manned-Vessel Single-Beam Echosounder Surveys for Bathymetry in a Coastal Environment
content: Unmanned surface vessels (USVs) are increasingly used for nearshore bathymetry, yet their interchangeability with manned-vessel surveys is rarely tested on identical lines. We compared single-beam echosounder surveys from a 1.4 m USV and a 3 m manned vessel over 13,287 m² of a shallow estuarine canal entrance in Queensland, Australia, using the same 8 m transects and real-time kinematic positioning on consecutive days. Agreement at 191 co-located samples was assessed using robust statistics, transect-clustered bootstrap confidence intervals (CIs), spatial autocorrelation and the International Hydrographic Organization (IHO) S-44 Order 1a total vertical uncertainty. Neither the bias (0.06 m; 95% CI −0.03 to 0.14 m) nor the net volume difference (30 ± 2600 m³) differed significantly from zero, but the 95% limits of agreement spanned −0.66 to 0.78 m. Differences were largest at the shallow survey margin (mean 0.39 m) and were spatially correlated over about 50 m, more than halving the effective sample size. Compliance with the combined Order 1a allowance (93–100% by depth range) could not be distinguished statistically from the 95% criterion. The USV surveyed three times faster, but the resulting level of detection of about 0.7 m means mixed-platform monitoring requires overlap surveys, crosslines and positioning quality control.
